problem: Prior robot navigation among pedestrians handles physical collision avoidance or generic social norms, but ignores pedestrians' emotional states; facial-only emotion perception is unreliable when faces are occluded, distant or turned away.
motivation: Emotions strongly predict human behavior and comfort, so a socially acceptable robot should adapt its behavior to them. Trajectories are an implicit, always-available channel that can complement faces, enabling emotion-dependent proxemic constraints in crowds.
key_idea: Estimate pedestrian emotion (happy/sad/angry/neutral) by fusing a trajectory-based linear emotion model (TEM, from motion-model parameters) with a face CNN, then map emotion to comfort/reachability distances used as constraints in a GVO-based navigation planner.
insight: Trajectory parameters (planning horizon, radius, preferred speed) linearly predict perceived emotion (85.33% 10-fold CV accuracy on only 23 videos), giving an emotion signal when faces are unavailable. The fusion weights face emotion by confidence and falls back to trajectory-only. Navigation results show proxemic constraints cost under 25% extra travel time while avoiding intrusions, but there is no ablation of fusion or any comparison to other socially-aware planners.
method: TEM (Trajectory-based Emotion Model): multiple linear regression from motion-model parameters P=[planning horizon, effective radius, preferred speed] to emotion vector [happy, angry, sad], fit on MTurk labels (100 participants, 23 simulated corridor videos, 5-point Likert).
Motion parameter estimation: pedestrian trackers plus Ensemble Kalman Filter and EM (Bayesian inference) estimate each pedestrian's motion parameters from noisy trajectories.

Facial emotion CNN: Xception-style fully-convolutional network with 4 residual depth-wise separable conv blocks, trained on FER-2013 (35,887 images) for four classes, on 48x48 face crops from the robot camera.

Joint emotion model: reliability-weighted average of trajectory and face emotions using tracking confidence alpha and a max-face-confidence rounding term; uses trajectory only if no face is available; label by threshold theta=0.55.
Emotion-aware path prediction: emotion bounds P_lb/P_ub (gamma=5%) clamp the estimated motion parameters; the GLMP algorithm then predicts pedestrian paths.

Proxemic constraints: emotion-specific comfort (hard) and reachability (soft) distances from Ruggiero et al. (e.g. sad 112.71/148.97 cm, happy 90.04/127.38 cm) added to Generalized Velocity Obstacles to compute the robot's new velocity.

setting.backbone: Xception-style CNN (trained on FER-2013) + linear regression TEM + Bayesian EnKF/EM + GVO planner
setting.training_data: FER-2013 (35,887 grayscale face images, 4 classes used); MTurk labels for 23 simulated walking videos (100 participants)
setting.observation: fixed overhead camera for trajectories + onboard robot RGB camera for faces
setting.action_space: continuous velocity via Generalized Velocity Obstacles
setting.simulator: custom crowd simulation replaying trajectories from real video datasets; real Pepper robot in lab
setting.privileged: overhead camera for pedestrian trajectories (assumed perspective-corrected); acted emotions from participants

numbers_note: Not a standard VLN/ObjNav benchmark. Table also reports NDLS-2 (21.08%/26), NPLC-1 (16.71%/30), NPLC-3 (18.93%/22), Students (9.12%/16), seq_hotel (11.89%/9), Street (11.09%/13); only two rows are listed here. Real-robot results were qualitative (11 participants).
results: TEM reaches 85.33% emotion accuracy in cross-validation on 23 labeled videos. In simulation on eight real crowd datasets the robot avoids 9-31 proxemic intrusions per dataset with under 25% (9.12-24.89%) extra travel time relative to non-social GVO. On the real Pepper robot, 11 participants reported comfort and perceived subtle reactions such as wider berth for sad and quicker yielding for angry.
limitations: Tiny emotion dataset (23 simulated videos) with acted emotions; no ablation of face/trajectory fusion and no baseline comparison beyond non-social GVO.
Requires an overhead camera for trajectories plus a robot camera for faces, both perspective corrected; only four emotions and low-to-medium density crowds.
Evaluation is mostly self-reported and uses intrusion counts and time overhead only; no cultural or group behavior modeling.
